before.detail: Examine the full body surface. Distinguish patch (non-infiltrated, flat), plaque (indurated, elevated), and tumor (solid nodule >1 cm depth) lesions.

before.prompt: What percentage of body surface area (BSA) is involved by patches/plaques?
before.detail: Use the rule-of-nines or palmar method (patient palm = ~1% BSA). Map and document all lesions. Assess at each visit for disease progression.

before.prompt: T1 disease. Is there clinically abnormal lymphadenopathy?
before.detail: T1: patch/plaque <10% BSA. Palpate all nodal basins. Lymph node >1.5 cm or palpably firm/fixed is abnormal.

before.prompt: T2 disease. Is there clinically abnormal lymphadenopathy?
before.detail: T2: patch/plaque ≥10% BSA. Lymph node assessment is mandatory. If nodes are suspicious on palpation or imaging, biopsy the most abnormal node.

before.prompt: T3 disease confirmed. Is there visceral involvement on imaging?
before.detail: T3: one or more skin tumors ≥1 cm. Obtain CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis (or PET-CT). Visceral involvement = M1.

Lymph node biopsy result (Dutch grade / NCI LN system)?
before.detail: N1: dermatopathic changes, no lymphoma (Dutch grade 1). N2: early involvement, rare Reed-Sternberg-like cells (Dutch grade 2). N3: partial/complete effacement (Dutch grade 3-4). N4: frank lymphoma involvement (Dutch grade 4).

before.prompt: N1/N2 lymph nodes. What is the T stage?

before.prompt: T1 N0. Assess peripheral blood for atypical cells or Sézary clone.
before.detail: In early-stage disease, blood involvement is uncommon but should be checked if there are suggestive clinical features (exfoliative erythroderma, pruritus). B0 = essentially no blood involvement.

before.detail: Stage IA: Patches or plaques on <10% BSA, no adenopathy, no visceral involvement, minimal or no blood involvement. Prognosis excellent; disease-specific survival near normal. Skin-directed therapy is standard first-line.
Stage IB: Patches or plaques on ≥10% BSA. Skin-directed therapy (NB-UVB, PUVA, topical steroids, mechlorethamine) with monitoring for progression. Median overall survival approximately 12 years.
Stage IIA: Patch/plaque (any BSA) with dermatopathic or early-involved lymph nodes. Combined skin-directed therapy; systemic agents (bexarotene, methotrexate) may be added for resistant disease.

Stage IIB: One or more skin tumors. Skin-directed therapy plus systemic agents. Brentuximab vedotin preferred if CD30 expression ≥10%. Mogamulizumab, bexarotene, IFN-alpha are options. Prognosis more guarded; median OS approximately 5 years.
Stage IVA1: Lymph node effacement (N3) without high blood burden. Aggressive systemic therapy warranted. Allogeneic HSCT may be considered in eligible patients with refractory disease.

before.prompt: Stage IVA2 / Sézary Syndrome (T1-T4 N0-N3 M0 B2)
before.detail: Stage IVA2: High blood burden (B2), fulfilling Sézary syndrome criteria when combined with erythroderma (T4). Extracorporeal photopheresis (ECP) is first-line for erythrodermic/Sézary disease. Mogamulizumab has demonstrated superior PFS vs vorinostat in this population. Allogeneic HSCT for fit patients.

before.prompt: Stage IVB (any T, any N, M1, any B)
before.detail: Stage IVB: Visceral (non-lymph node) involvement. Lung, liver, spleen most common. Systemic chemotherapy (gemcitabine, liposomal doxorubicin, CHOP-based regimens) or clinical trial preferred. Median survival <2 years; allogeneic SCT considered in eligible patients.

rationale: Separate syndrome diagnosis from legacy surrogate thresholds.
before: DEFINING FEATURE: B2 criteria required — Sézary cells >1000/mcL OR CD4:CD8 >10 OR CD4+CD7- >40% OR CD4+CD26- >30% PLUS clonal TCR in blood

rationale: Correct an invalid immunostain-only distinction.

rationale: Do not require CD30 for large-cell transformation.

after: Usually CD3+/CD4+ with aberrant T-cell antigen loss; variants occur. Large-cell transformation may be CD30-positive or CD30-negative.

rationale: Correct trial identity, combination regimen, and maintenance timing.

rationale: Correct survival-versus-mortality inversion and avoid unbounded whole-body treatment.

after: The 2002 trial used clobetasol 40 g/day initially. In extensive BP, one-year survival was 76% with topical treatment versus 58% with oral prednisone—not mortality of 41% versus 58%. before.title: Hair Pull Test
before.markdown:
-   **Technique:** Gently grasp ~50 hairs and pull from proximal to distal.
-   **Interpretation:** Pulling >10% of hairs (~5 hairs) suggests an active shedding process (positive test), characteristic of Telogen or Anagen Effluvium.

after.title: Hair Pull Test
after.markdown: Gently pull a small bundle of hairs and document site, technique, and number removed. The historical >10% cutoff is not universal: a study of 181 healthy participants found 97.2% had two or fewer hairs removed. An increased result supports active shedding but does not identify its cause.

rationale: Same hair-pull correction in workup representation.
before: Positive: ≥6 hairs (>10%) shed → active shedding.
after: Record number and scalp site. A healthy-volunteer study found ≤2 hairs in 97.2%; the historical >10% threshold is not a universal diagnostic cutoff.

after.markdown: Topical minoxidil is an established option; strength and application schedule depend on the product and population. Low-dose oral minoxidil is off-label for alopecia and requires individualized cardiovascular, renal, pregnancy, and interaction assessment. In a 24-week randomized trial in men, oral 5 mg daily did not demonstrate superiority over topical 5% twice daily for the primary hair-density outcomes.

before.title: Oral Systemics
before.markdown:
Still important options.

-   **Methotrexate:** A cost-effective choice for skin and joints.
-   **Apremilast:** Oral option with a favorable safety profile (no lab monitoring).
-   **Deucravacitinib:** A newer oral selective TYK2 inhibitor with efficacy comparable to some biologics.

after.title: Oral Systemics
after.markdown: Oral options include methotrexate, apremilast and selective TYK2 inhibition. Selection requires agent-specific efficacy, adverse-effect, reproductive and monitoring assessment. Neither absence of routine laboratory requirements for one drug nor efficacy in one trial establishes superiority or safety equivalence to a biologic class.

rationale: Correct menthol receptor and distinguish investigational H4 biology from standard antihistamines.

before.title: Receptors on Nerve Endings
before.markdown:
-   **Histamine Receptors (H1R, H4R):** Target for antihistamines.
-   **IL-31 Receptor (OSMRβ/IL31RA):** Target for nemolizumab.
-   **PAR-2:** Receptor for proteases like tryptase.
-   **TRP Channels (TRPV1, TRPA1):** Ion channels that modulate itch and are activated by capsaicin, menthol, and other stimuli.

after.title: Receptors on Nerve Endings
after.markdown: Conventional antihistamines used for histaminergic itch chiefly block H1 receptors; H4-directed treatment is not interchangeable with routine H1 treatment. Nemolizumab targets IL-31 receptor alpha. Capsaicin activates TRPV1; menthol chiefly activates the cold-sensitive TRPM8 channel. Receptor involvement does not establish efficacy of a drug for every itch syndrome.

rationale: Avoid psychiatric diagnosis solely from a negative somatic workup.

before.title: Psychogenic Pruritus
before.markdown: Itch related to a primary psychiatric disorder. This is a diagnosis of exclusion. Includes conditions like delusional infestation.

after.title: Psychogenic Pruritus
after.markdown: Psychological and psychiatric factors can cause, amplify, or coexist with itch. A psychogenic attribution requires appropriate positive clinical criteria and evaluation for other causes; normal tests alone do not establish it. Delusional infestation requires assessment of the fixed belief and possible secondary causes.

before.name: Group I — Pruritus on diseased / inflamed skin
before.detail: Primary skin lesions visible; itch is a consequence of skin inflammation or structural change.

children.name: Atopic Dermatitis
children.detail: IL-4/IL-13 axis; Th2-skewed inflammation; filaggrin barrier defects. Hallmark: flexural itch, relapsing course.

children.name: Psoriasis vulgaris
children.detail: IL-17A/IL-23 axis; itch present in >60% of patients; often underreported. Biologic therapies reduce itch scores.

children.name: Lichen Planus
children.detail: Lichenoid T-cell reaction; violaceous polygonal papules; mucosal involvement common.

children.name: Contact Dermatitis (Allergic / Irritant)
children.detail: Delayed type IV hypersensitivity (allergic) or direct epidermal damage (irritant). Patch testing essential for allergic type.

children.name: Urticaria (chronic spontaneous)
children.detail: Transient wheals <24h; autoimmune IgG against FcεRI or IgE in 40-50%. Omalizumab second-line.

children.name: Scabies
children.detail: Sarcoptes scabiei var hominis; interdigital burrows; nocturnal predominance; treat household simultaneously.

children.name: Candidiasis (cutaneous / vulvovaginal)
children.detail: Macerated intertriginous erythema with satellite pustules; KOH prep confirms. Topical azoles first-line.

children.name: Pediculosis (head / pubic lice)
children.detail: Nits on hair shafts; pubic lice in anogenital region. Permethrin or malathion topically.

children.name: Varicella / VZV (reactivation)
children.detail: Vesicular rash following dermatome (zoster). Postherpetic itch can persist months after lesion resolution.

children.name: Bullous Pemphigoid
children.detail: Anti-BP180 (NC16A domain) + anti-BP230 IgG antibodies. Tense bullae on urticarial base; intense pruritus often precedes blistering.

children.name: Dermatitis Herpetiformis (DH)
children.detail: IgA anti-transglutaminase deposition at DEJ; gluten-sensitive enteropathy; granular IgA on DIF is pathognomonic. Dapsone + gluten-free diet.

children.name: Lichen Sclerosus
children.detail: Figure-of-eight vulval/perianal distribution; sclerotic white plaques; 4-5% SCC risk with long-term disease.

children.name: Mycosis Fungoides (CTCL)
children.detail: Most common CTCL; patch → plaque → tumor stage; pruritus may be the dominant symptom for years before diagnosis.

children.name: Mastocytosis (Cutaneous)
children.detail: Urticaria pigmentosa: tan-brown macules/papules that urticates with stroking (Darier sign). Serum tryptase elevated in systemic disease.

before.name: Group II — Pruritus on non-diseased skin
before.detail: Skin appears normal; itch driven by systemic disease, drugs, or metabolic derangements.

children.name: CKD-Associated Pruritus (formerly uremic pruritus)
children.detail: Affects 40-70% of hemodialysis patients. Uremic toxins + κ-opioid dysregulation + small-fiber neuropathy. Difelikefalin (κ-opioid agonist) FDA-approved 2021.

children.name: Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC)
children.detail: AMA+ (>95%); elevated ALP/GGT; palmar-plantar itch worst at night. Cholestyramine, rifampin, naltrexone.

children.name: Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC)
children.detail: Multi-focal biliary strictures; associated with IBD (especially UC); MRCP for diagnosis.

children.name: Intrahepatic Cholestasis of Pregnancy (ICP)
children.detail: Third trimester; elevated bile acids; fetal risk (stillbirth). Ursodeoxycholic acid + early delivery at 36-37 weeks.

children.name: Drug-Induced Cholestasis
children.detail: Anabolic steroids, OCPs, amoxicillin-clavulanate, chlorpromazine; latency 1-12 weeks.

children.name: Hodgkin Lymphoma
children.detail: Cytokine-mediated (IL-31, IL-6, TARC); pruritus may precede diagnosis by years; resolves with effective chemotherapy.

children.name: Polycythemia Vera / MPN
children.detail: Aquagenic pruritus: burning stinging within minutes of water contact. JAK2 V617F in 95%. Ruxolitinib for refractory pruritus.

children.name: Iron-Deficiency Anemia
children.detail: Iron deficiency can cause generalized pruritus even before anemia develops. Ferritin <15 ng/mL diagnostic. Iron repletion curative.

children.name: Thyroid Disease (hypo- and hyperthyroidism)
children.detail: Hypothyroidism: xerosis-driven itch. Hyperthyroidism: vasodilation + sweating-driven itch. TSH is first-line screen.

children.name: Diabetes Mellitus
children.detail: Generalized pruritus via peripheral neuropathy and nephrogenic causes. Glycemic control + emollients + gabapentinoids.

children.name: Hyperparathyroidism (secondary in CKD)
children.detail: PTH-driven calcium-phosphate deposition in skin nerves contributes to uremic pruritus component.

children.name: Opioids
children.detail: Mu-opioid receptor-mediated; most intense with spinal opioids. Treat with nalbuphine (mixed κ-agonist/μ-antagonist) or low-dose naltrexone.

children.name: ACE Inhibitors
children.detail: Bradykinin accumulation; may present as pruritus without angioedema. Switch to ARB.

children.name: Statins / Chloroquine / Hydroxyurea
children.detail: Cholestatic mechanism (statins) or direct mast cell stimulation (chloroquine). Hydroxyurea causes prurigo-like papules.

children.name: Checkpoint Inhibitors (immunotherapy)
children.detail: Pembrolizumab, nivolumab, atezolizumab; immune-related adverse events including pruritus in 10-25%; grade 3 pruritus managed with systemic steroids.

before.name: Group III — Pruritus with chronic scratch lesions
before.detail: Primary cause may be resolved or unclear; dominant feature is established secondary lesions from chronic scratching.

children.name: Lichen Simplex Chronicus (LSC)
children.detail: Itch-scratch cycle causes lichenification. Common sites: nape of neck, ankles, anogenital. Potent topical steroids under occlusion; habit reversal therapy.

children.name: Prurigo Nodularis
children.detail: Multiple hyperkeratotic papules/nodules on trunk and extremities. Intense itch drives chronic scratching. Dupilumab (FDA-approved 2022) and nemolizumab (IL-31Rα) are targeted therapies. PMID 23614588.

before.name: Group IV — Neuropathic Pruritus
before.detail: Itch originating from peripheral or central nervous system pathology; no primary skin lesion; dermatomal or localized distribution with sensory abnormalities.

children.name: Brachioradial Pruritus
children.detail: Cervical radiculopathy (C5-C8); lateral forearm/dorsal arm; aggravated by UV (sun exposure); ice pack test positive. MRI cervical spine. Gabapentin, capsaicin.

children.name: Notalgia Paresthetica
children.detail: T2-T6 dorsal nerve entrapment at paraspinal muscles; interscapular itch; hyperpigmented patch at left/right paraspinal region. Capsaicin, gabapentin, physical therapy, botulinum toxin.

children.name: Post-Herpetic Itch
children.detail: Chronic itch in healed herpes zoster dermatome; distinct from postherpetic neuralgia; allodynia and burning common. High-dose capsaicin patch (8%), gabapentinoids, TCAs.

children.name: Small-Fiber Neuropathy (SFN)
children.detail: Reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density on skin biopsy; idiopathic or diabetes-associated; burning quality. Gabapentinoids, low-dose naltrexone, duloxetine.

children.name: Central Neuropathic Itch (MS, stroke, spinal cord)
children.detail: Multiple sclerosis: Lhermitte-type paroxysmal itch. Post-stroke or spinal cord injury: unilateral dermatomal itch. Gabapentinoids; low-dose opioid antagonists.

before.name: Group V — Psychogenic / Somatoform Pruritus
before.detail: Itch is driven by psychiatric illness; skin and systemic workup unrevealing; requires mental health co-management.

children.name: Delusions of Parasitosis (Delusional Infestation)
children.detail: Fixed delusion of skin infestation despite negative workup (matchbox sign). First-line: olanzapine or risperidone at low dose. Build therapeutic alliance; avoid confrontation. Do not use anti-parasitic treatments.

children.name: OCD-Spectrum / Neurotic Excoriations
children.detail: Repetitive skin picking driven by anxiety or OCD; skin lesions reflect behavioral rather than dermatologic cause. SSRIs + CBT (habit reversal training).

children.name: Somatoform Pruritus
children.detail: Somatic symptom disorder where itch is the dominant complaint. Full systemic workup negative. Multidisciplinary management (dermatology + psychiatry + CBT).

before.name: Group VI — Mixed / Multifactorial Pruritus
before.detail: Most common group in clinical practice; multiple overlapping etiologies (e.g., atopic + drug-induced, uremic + xerosis, neuropathic + psychogenic).

children.name: Pruritus of the Elderly (Senile Pruritus)
children.detail: Multifactorial: xerosis + epidermal thinning + nerve fiber reduction + comorbidities + polypharmacy. Most common cause in >65 age group. Emollients, gabapentin, mirtazapine, treat comorbidities.

children.name: Chronic Idiopathic Pruritus
children.detail: Diagnosis of exclusion after comprehensive workup (PMID 23614588). Emerging evidence for IL-31 pathway (nemolizumab) and substance P/NK1 pathway (aprepitant) in idiopathic cases.

rationale: Correct specimen/test error and avoid indiscriminate staging tests.
before: Pruritus may precede Hodgkin lymphoma diagnosis by months to years. Order: CBC with differential (look for eosinophilia, Reed-Sternberg cells), LDH, ESR, CRP, uric acid. CT chest/abdomen/pelvis or PET-CT. Biopsy enlarged lymph node. Pruritus in Hodgkin is cytokine-mediated (IL-31, IL-6, thymus and activation-regulated chemokine [TARC]).
after: Assess concerning constitutional symptoms, lymphadenopathy and examination findings with appropriate laboratory testing and specialist evaluation. Reed–Sternberg cells are assessed in tissue, not sought on a routine CBC. Imaging and tissue diagnosis are selected according to clinical suspicion.

rationale: Correct timing, specimen and repeat-dose omission.
before: Common causes: pinworm (Enterobius vermicularis — collect adhesive tape test at night), hemorrhoids, contact dermatitis (moist wipes, topical anesthetics), dietary irritants (coffee, spices). Treat underlying cause. Scotch tape test or stool O&P for pinworm; mebendazole 100mg × 1 if confirmed.
after: Evaluate irritant/allergic dermatitis, infection and anorectal causes. For suspected pinworm, collect perianal tape samples on three consecutive mornings before washing or toileting; stool O&P is generally low yield. CDC regimens include a second dose two weeks after the first; do not present a single dose as the complete regimen.

rationale: Cooling response and imaging do not establish the diagnosis by themselves.
before: Cervical radiculopathy (C5-C8) most common etiology; worsened by UV exposure. Ice pack test: relief with ice pack confirms neuropathic origin. MRI cervical spine. First-line: gabapentin/pregabalin, topical capsaicin 0.075%, sunscreen. Cervical traction or surgery if structural cause confirmed. PMID 23614588.
after: A compatible distribution, sensory symptoms and cooling response support neuropathic itch but are not independently confirmatory. Consider neurologic examination and selective imaging when structural disease is suspected; treatment and procedural referral are individualized.

rationale: Remove obsolete and potentially pruritogenic treatment recommendation; distinguish diagnosis from serology.
before: Palmar/plantar pruritus, worst at night. Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) slows disease but may not relieve pruritus. Pruritus-specific: cholestyramine (first-line), rifampin, naltrexone, sertraline. Obeticholic acid + bezafibrate as second-line options. PMID 23614588.
after: Correlate cholestatic liver tests, disease-specific serology and imaging; AMA alone does not establish the cause of itch. Use hepatology-directed PBC and antipruritic treatment. Linerixibat received U.S. approval in March 2026 for PBC-associated cholestatic pruritus; do not retain an outdated blanket investigational label or recommend obeticholic acid as an itch treatment.

rationale: Correct test interpretation and prevent blanket laboratory/biopsy protocols.

before.title: Lymphomatoid Papulosis (LyP)
before.content:
• Epidemiology: Incidence 1.2-1.9 per million/year. Median age 45. M:F 1.5:1. Can occur at any age (including children).
  • Manifestations: Recurrent crops of 3-100 papulonodules that necrotize centrally, resolve in 3-12 weeks leaving scars. Continuous eruption of new lesions.
  • Histologic Types: A (most common): CD30+ cells with neutrophils/eosinophils. B: MF-like. C: ALCL-like. D: CD8+ epidermotropic. E: angioinvasive (worse prognosis). F: folliculotropic.
  • Associated Lymphomas: 10-20% lifetime risk (highest in first 10 years). MF (most common), pcALCL, Hodgkin. Type E = higher risk.
  • Management: Often none needed. Options: topical steroids, phototherapy, low-dose MTX (10-25mg/week, best for suppression). Avoid aggressive therapy.
  • Prognosis: 5-year survival >99%. Does not affect life expectancy unless secondary lymphoma develops.

before.title: Oral Systemics
before.content:
Still important options.
  • Methotrexate: A cost-effective choice for skin and joints.
  • Apremilast: Oral option with a favorable safety profile (no lab monitoring).
  • Deucravacitinib: A newer oral selective TYK2 inhibitor with efficacy comparable to some biologics.

after.title: Oral Systemics
after.content: Oral options include methotrexate, apremilast and selective TYK2 inhibition. Selection requires agent-specific efficacy, adverse-effect, reproductive and monitoring assessment. Neither absence of routine laboratory requirements for one drug nor efficacy in one trial establishes superiority or safety equivalence to a biologic class.
